refuted.summary: Skill promotion rewards executions with zero policy denials, encouraging skills to avoid attempted denials rather than proving intended behavior: a correctly constrained skill that triggers a denial on hostile input is penalized, while a no-op or narrowly exercised malicious skill accumulates clean runs.
refuted.reasoning:
The finding imports an enforcement model this architecture does not use, and the "inversion" dissolves once the denial semantics are read in context.

1. Who fires the denial. In this contract, skills are *subjects*, not policy enforcers. Denials are emitted by the trust-plane kernel against the skill's own action attempts (§10 hooks E/F: egress and execute are deny-by-default decisions over the skill's requests; §11.4: "The runtime's good behavior is never the control; the kernel is"). There is no event in this architecture where a "correctly constrained skill triggers a denial on hostile input" as intended behavior — a skill refusing hostile input produces no denial at all (it simply doesn't attempt the action); a *denial* means the skill itself attempted something outside its whitelist. So "zero policy denials" = "the skill never attempted an unauthorized action during supervised runs," which is a least-privilege behavioral-conformance check, exactly aligned with the deny-by-default doctrine (§2.4) — not inverted.

2. The doc already equates denial with violation — the recommendation's distinction doesn't exist here. §9.2 line 197: "**Policy violation at runtime:** a skill whose execution triggers a policy denial is demoted to quarantine pending review." In this model a runtime denial *is* the definition of a policy violation by the skill-as-subject. The recommendation to "change the metric to zero policy violations (denials of intended capabilities)" is asking for what the text already means; "denial of an intended capability" can't occur mid-run for declared capabilities because hook F gates invocation on declared capabilities ⊆ persona + task whitelist before execution starts.

3. The hostile-input scenario is actually the case where non-promotion is correct. If hostile input can drive a skill to attempt a denied action, the skill is injectable — the kernel denying is the defense working, and refusing to raise that skill's trust tier (demote-pending-review, §9.2) is the right response, not a penalty error.

4. The residual half-truth — "clean-run counts measure exercise breadth, not safety" (a narrowly-exercised or dormant-malicious skill accumulates clean runs) — is real but bounded by the architecture and already tracked: (a) promotion never exempts a skill from the kernel — hooks E/F enforce the declared-minimal capability whitelist at *every* invocation at every tier, so a time-bomb skill's blast radius is bounded by its least-privilege capability set regardless of tier; (b) any later denial demotes to quarantine automatically (§9.2); (c) the gate also requires supervised execution, least-privilege capability review, and signature — the run count is not the sole control; (d) how N should scale per capability class is an explicitly open review item (§14 Q2, cross-referenced from §9.1's own text at line 188). Suggesting adversarial/edge-case test coverage as part of N's definition is legitimate input to §14 Q2 — a discussion contribution, not a defect in the stated metric.

One genuine residual edge survives at low grade: context-dependent denials (e.g., a task-scoped egress allowlist differing between runs) could demote a behaviorally-correct skill — but that fails conservative (false-positive demotion "pending review," recoverable), which is the safe direction in this threat model, not a security inversion.

Verdict: refuted — the quoted evidence is misread (denial ≠ a skill's successful defensive act here; it is by the doc's own definition a violation by the skill), and the residual coverage concern is already addressed by continuing runtime enforcement (§10), automatic demotion (§9.2), and the tracked open question (§14 Q2).
